texts.151g-P6eP7f:
What impressed me most was their form of authority, mandar obedeciendo, which is leading by obeying. The representatives are in charge of carrying out what the assemblies decided, and they have to answer to the people who gave them the mandate.

The Zapatistas are also the closest thing to a whole example that I found, because their autonomy goes beyond how they vote. They've set up their own education and health care, and their own justice. They run their own collective production and political training. They've also worked out their own ways of teaching outsiders, all while coordinating beyond a single village.

texts.151g-P9fP10d:
After a long internal review, in 2023, the Zapatistas announced they were dissolving the Rebel Zapatista Autonomous Municipalities and the Good Government Juntas. Their new arrangement moved authority toward a Local Autonomous Government in each community. Those local governments can coordinate through regional collectives, but the coordinating levels are explicitly described as depending on the communities instead of sitting above them.

Most institutions end up with more and more layers and offices as they get older. The Zapatistas took stock of theirs, and they moved authority down. They didn't write a leadership book and open up a certification program, they changed the system they were actually living in.

This is also where I have to rein in my enthusiasm. Zapatista autonomy grew out of Indigenous communities with long histories. They share language and family ties. texts.151g-P13d: They also don't prove my whole economic path, the one where unpriced internal necessities come first, then a common purse, and then you get rid of outside money. Zapatista communities do use collective work to support their schools and clinics. They support their autonomous government and their resistance that way too. But they also sell products and trade, and they get support from outside. What they do show is that major necessities and public functions can be taken out of ordinary market purchase and governed collectively. Outside help can build capability. It can also create gatekeepers, and uneven dependence, when the specialist or the donor or the organization stays indispensable.

texts.151g-P15f: One way an escuelita could fail is if it becomes a business, where residents' lives turn into a performance of community for paying outsiders, and success gets measured by how many people come instead of how many daughter communities get started. A week of feeling transformed isn't what it's for. It's for teaching enough of the social and material system that some people can build it somewhere else.

texts.151g-P14xP15f:
As part of celebrating the 10th anniversary of their autonomous governments, the Zapatistas opened up the Escuelita. Outsiders would live with families and learn autonomy by participating in the day to day life there. The first sessions had about 1,500 students, and later sessions had thousands more.

One way an escuelita could fail is if it becomes a business, where residents' lives turn into a performance of community for paying outsiders, and success gets measured by how many people come instead of how many daughter communities get started. A week of feeling transformed isn't what it's for. It's for teaching enough of the social and material system that some people can build it somewhere else.
texts.151g-P14y2P15f:
In celebration of the 10th anniversary of their autonomous governments, the Zapatistas opened up the Escuelita, where outsiders came to live with families and learn autonomy by taking part in day to day life. The first sessions had about 1,500 students; later ones had thousands more.

One way an escuelita could fail is if it becomes a business, where residents' lives turn into a performance of community for paying outsiders, and success gets measured by how many people come instead of how many daughter communities get started. A week of feeling transformed isn't what it's for. It's for teaching enough of the social and material system that some people can build it somewhere else.
texts.151g-P16aP17d:
In my research I also looked into what came out of the Escuelita. There are alumni networks, and people took practices home and organized later. But I couldn't find a clean chain from one Escuelita student to a new communal institution, with evidence of how its members and their kids actually did over time. And Zapatista influence was spreading internationally before the Escuelita, so a later resemblance doesn't prove it came from there. So I'm borrowing a way of teaching and the ambition to replicate it. I'm not claiming the Zapatistas already proved my whole model.

Sociocracy has a very different history, but it got to some similar forms, like circles, consent, distributed authority, and links between levels. That resemblance doesn't prove a universal formula. But it gives builders another serious system to study, so they're not inventing their governance during their first dispute.
